lead: How robots plan steps and try to anticipate physical motion.

news.title: Google opens a cloud planning layer for robot tasks
news.summary: On October 27 Google Cloud opened public-preview access to Gemini Robotics ER 2, a model that interprets video, plans steps and calls separate robot-control tools.
news.details: The calls use APIs, defined interfaces between software components. The model can interpret video, choose a navigation or manipulation function and check progress. Coordinating specialized components in this way is called orchestration. Google also describes cooperation between robots, but the actual behavior still depends on their hardware and control systems.
news.technical_novelty: High-level reasoning coordinates perception, progress checks and robot software interfaces.
news.engineering_impact: Useful for experimenting with multi-step tasks, but not a replacement for local motion control.
news.limitations: Cloud preview is not a guarantee of safe or reliable autonomous deployment.
news.evidence_status: Official availability announcement with developer-reported metrics.
news.body:
A request like 'find the box and bring it here' hides many decisions. A robot must choose a route, pick up the object and check whether each step succeeded. On October 27, Google Cloud announced public-preview access to Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2, a high-level model that plans these steps and calls separate robot-control programs.

The calls use APIs, defined interfaces between software components. The model can interpret video, choose a navigation or manipulation function and check progress. Coordinating specialized components in this way is called orchestration. Google also describes cooperation between robots, but the actual behavior still depends on their hardware and control systems.

Google reports 91.3% accuracy for locating a critical moment in video, with a mean timing error of 0.96 seconds. That is a specific video-understanding benchmark, not a general robot task-success rate. The model existed before October; the new event is its cloud availability. Network delays, disconnections and emergency stops remain practical engineering responsibilities.

news.title: Can a robot predict how the scene will move?
news.summary: Researchers introduced WorldFlow on October 29, predicting future video and 3D point motion; average displacement error on SpatialCog was 0.060 m.
news.details: The researchers trained the model on 1.44 million object-level samples from simulated and real scenes. WorldFlowBench, their evaluation collection, contains 1,678 samples from 11 sources. On SpatialCog, average displacement error was 0.060 metres, a 54.2% reduction relative to the strongest external method in the authors' comparison.
news.technical_novelty: Video prediction and three-dimensional motion forecasting are learned jointly.
news.engineering_impact: Such forecasts could help robots choose actions.
news.limitations: This is not a demonstrated general-purpose robot controller.
news.body:
When you watch a ball move, you can imagine where it will be a moment later. A robot has a harder version of that problem: it needs to anticipate both the image and the geometry of motion. WorldFlow, introduced on October 29, predicts future video frames and the trajectories of selected points in three-dimensional space.

The researchers trained the model on 1.44 million object-level samples from simulated and real scenes. WorldFlowBench, their evaluation collection, contains 1,678 samples from 11 sources. On SpatialCog, average displacement error was 0.060 metres, a 54.2% reduction relative to the strongest external method in the authors' comparison.

That does not mean a robot will always catch a ball or move an object safely. Predicting motion and selecting safe physical actions are different tasks. Real use would require checks on computation speed, camera accuracy and behavior in unexpected environments.
